The same meaning and purpose applies to the second oath:

﴿By the heaven with its intricate pathways﴾ (Wal-sama'i dhat al-hubuk)...

Here Allah swears by the heaven, whose structure is firm and well-ordered, like the links of a coat of mail, arranged with great precision. Sometimes the clouds in the sky appear in exactly this form: they look like woven chain-mail, rippled in patterns like waves of water over which the wind blows at a steady pace. It is also possible that the orbits within the heavens are meant, because these orbits are such that, if they were shown by coloured lines, they would look like the rings of a coat of mail. Swearing by this heaven, built in such an excellent manner, Allah says that your statements about the Resurrection are not consistent. There is turmoil in your arguments. They have neither firmness nor stability. Rather, your words reflect bewilderment and confusion. Whoever wishes may be overwhelmed by these words, and whoever wishes may cling to them. Not only do they lack any stability or steadiness, but they are always made up of bewilderment, anguish and uncertainty, and that is always the nature of a false position: unsettled, changing, and shifting from day to day. Falsehood is always wandering aimlessly. It has neither signposts on its path nor any light by which one could walk the road properly. Moreover, falsehood has no principle; it wavers, because it has no firm foundation and no fixed measure. Even if the people of falsehood at some time unite on a matter, after a while they fall to fighting one another, and disputes and enmities remain among them.

The turmoil of the people of falsehood, their disagreement and their hesitant thoughts become even clearer when they are viewed in the light of the heavenly order, which is extremely firm, whose links are joined to one another and well arranged.

This statement continues. It is said that these people live not merely in conjecture and estimation, but in a world of illusion. Their views about the Hereafter are not derived from truth and certainty. The truth is entirely manifest, but their thoughts on this subject are scattered. Then a scene of their scattered thinking is presented, one that the eyes seem to see as though it were running on a screen.

Sometimes the clouds in the sky appear in exactly this form: they look like woven chain-mail, rippled in patterns like waves of water over which the wind blows at a steady pace. It is also possible that the orbits within the heavens are meant, because these orbits are such that, if they were shown by coloured lines, they would look like the rings of a coat of mail. Swearing by this heaven, built in such an excellent manner, Allah says that your statements about the Resurrection are not consistent. There is turmoil in your arguments. They have neither firmness nor stability. Rather, your words reflect bewilderment and confusion. Whoever wishes may be overwhelmed by these words, and whoever wishes may cling to them. Not only do they lack any stability or steadiness, but they are always made up of bewilderment, anguish and uncertainty, and that is always the nature of a false position: unsettled, changing, and shifting from day to day. Falsehood is always wandering aimlessly. It has neither signposts on its path nor any light by which one could walk the road properly. Moreover, falsehood has no principle; it wavers, because it has no firm foundation and no fixed measure. Even if the people of falsehood at some time unite on a matter, after a while they fall to fighting one another, and disputes and enmities remain among them.

The turmoil of the people of falsehood, their disagreement and their hesitant thoughts become even clearer when they are viewed in the light of the heavenly order, which is extremely firm, whose links are joined to one another and well arranged.

This statement continues. It is said that these people live not merely in conjecture and estimation, but in a world of illusion. Their views about the Hereafter are not derived from truth and certainty. The truth is entirely manifest, but their thoughts on this subject are scattered. Then a scene of their scattered thinking is presented, one that the eyes seem to see as though it were running on a screen.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 51, verse 10:

"Qutila" ... "tus'jiluun"

Kharrs means conjecture, supposition and estimation, that is, a way of thinking that is not based on any deep and certain standard and has no sound premise or conclusion. Allah pronounces a curse upon such people, that they be killed, and the meaning of a curse from Allah is: "They are simply destroyed."

Qutilal-kharrasoon (51:1) ["Killed are the conjecturers,"] and their state is explained a little further.

Those who are immersed in ignorance and heedlessly intoxicated (الذين ... ساهون, 51:11). Their thinking is saturated with false notions, and they are intoxicated with delusions. They neither come to their senses nor wake up. The manner of expression gives a particular colour and image. Their picture is something like this: they are lying in heedlessness, as if asleep or unconscious, lost in a stupor, and they have no awareness of their surroundings. They do not reflect on anything, and their minds and intellects do not function, as though they were intoxicated. For they cannot grasp even a plain matter, one which any person of sound understanding would comprehend the moment they see it, and this is their condition.

﴿They ask, "When will the Day of Recompense come?"﴾ (51:21) The manner in which they ask shows that their purpose is not to seek knowledge or understanding. Rather, they are deniers who reject it, and they ask as if it were an impossible matter, because the word "أيان" (ayyan, "when") is used on such occasions.

For this reason, the Qur'an, in its own manner, quickly shows a glimpse of the Resurrection, as if to say: "Look, this is what you consider impossible." They are burned in it in the way that a metal is heated in fire to determine its true nature.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 51, verse 13:

"On the Day they will be burned over the Fire" (51:13). "On the Day they will be tormented over the Fire." And in that very scene they are also humiliated, which adds to their anguish, though they are already in distress.

The passage is from Sayyid Qutb's commentary, and the system instructions require translating Urdu into English. Here is the translation.

"Taste your trial; this is what you were demanding to be hastened." [Qur'an 51:14]... This was the fitting answer, and for heedless people sunk in stupor and deep sleep, this severity is most appropriate and in keeping with the scene. For this reason Allah invoked a curse upon them, in the harshest manner: so they are destroyed, and they will be heated in the Fire the way metal is heated so that its dross may be separated from it.

Now let us turn to the opposing party, to another platform, and turn over the second page of the book. There stands the other party, who does not speak of mere illusions and whose words are not wavering. They are the God-conscious (muttaqun), not the arrogant. They are awake, they worship, they seek forgiveness, and they do not waste their lives in stupor.

These are the God-fearing, grouped together. They are the ones who stay awake (in worship at night). They have a keen sense that Allah is watching them. They are also sensitive about their own selves. These people—

﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in gardens and springs﴾ (51:15) "they will be in gardens and springs," and...

"Taking that which their Lord has given them, joyfully" (51:16). ﴿Taking what their Lord has given them﴾ — they will be receiving the bounties and favours of their Lord as the reward for the deeds they performed in the life of this world. They worshipped Him as though they were seeing Him, and in the belief that He was seeing them.

﴿Indeed, they were before that, good-doers﴾ (51:16). They were righteous people before the arrival of that Day, and the picture of their goodness is very captivating, extremely bright and sensitive:

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 51, verses 17–18:

"They used to sleep little at night, and in the last hours of the night they would seek forgiveness." They stay awake in the last part of the night while people sleep. They turn to their Lord in repentance and seeking forgiveness, and they ask Allah for mercy. They dose very little and sleep very little. In the darkness of the night they converse with their Lord. Their sides move away from their beds, the longing to look toward Allah lightens them, and sleep cannot weigh down their bodies.

Imam Hasan al-Basri says:

"﴿Kanu qalilan min al-layli ma yahja'un﴾ (51:17)" meaning: they perform the night prayer with effort; they sleep little at night, they spent the night in action, and they extended their standing (in prayer) until morning, so that the seeking of forgiveness came at dawn.

Qatadah narrates from Ahnaf ibn Qays:

"﴿Kanu qalilan min al-layli ma yahja'un﴾" meaning: they slept little, and then he said, "I am not among the people of this verse."

Hasan al-Basri says that Ahnaf ibn Qays used to say: "My deeds were presented alongside the deeds of the people of Paradise, and it became clear that they are such people that there is a great difference between them and us, since we cannot reach their deeds. These were the people who slept little at night. Then I presented my deeds alongside the deeds of the people of Hell, and there was no goodness among the people of Hell. They denied the Book of Allah and denied the Resurrection and the gathering. I saw that those people too are better than us, those who did some good deeds and also some bad deeds."

Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said: a man of the Banu Tamim said to my father, "Abu Usama, there is a quality that is not in us; Allah has mentioned a people..."

"﴿Kanu qalilan min al-layli ma yahja'un﴾ (51:17)" — "those who used to sleep little at night" — they long for it and consider themselves lowly in comparison. Nevertheless, Allah has chosen for this station some people in the Ummah who fulfil the right of these verses, and because of them they are recorded among the muhsinun (the people of excellence) in the sight of Allah. This is their relationship with their Lord; as for their relationship with people, it is that relationship which befits a righteous person.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 51, verse 19:

...and in their wealth there was a right for the beggar and the deprived (51:19). They set aside a share of their wealth for the one who asks and is given, and they also fix a right for the deprived person who remains silent, keeps his modesty, and goes without. They hold a right in their wealth for both kinds of people. They impose this right upon themselves, and this right is unlimited, not fixed.

This indication is in harmony with the central theme of the Surah, in which it is stated that sustenance is in the heavens, so that human hearts may be freed somewhat from stinginess, miserliness, and absorption in gathering wealth night and day. It is also an introduction to the important part of the Surah, and it is at the same time the final touch of the portrait of the God-conscious (muttaqun) and the doers of good (muhsinun).

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 51, verse 20:

Through this verse, attention is drawn to the signs present in the horizons and within the self, and it is said that the means of sustenance appointed for you are determined from the heavens. Allah swears by His own Being, and here the Divine Being is described as the Lord of the heaven and the earth, who were mentioned in this lesson; and the answer to the oath is this important matter, namely the resurrection and gathering.

﴿And in the earth are signs for those who have certainty. And in yourselves. Will you not then see?﴾ (51:20-21)

This small planet upon which we live is a very great exhibition hall, for the wonders and marvels that Allah has placed in it. Up to now, only a very few of the wonders of this world have been placed on display in this exhibition hall. New discoveries are revealed day after day, and new wonders come before us. Another exhibition hall of this kind is our own self: the human soul, its mysterious psychological world. Within this human being too are the secrets of this universe. Not only the secrets of the earth, but the secrets of the whole universe.

In these verses there is a brief indication to these two exhibition halls, that the doors of both these halls are being opened for you. But the benefit will be for the person who wishes to see them, who wishes to believe, and who wishes to fill his life with the blessings and joys, who wishes to gain knowledge, recognition, wisdom and lessons, through which his heart will come alive and his life will be increased.

Allah has framed His speech in such a way that people of every level among His creatures can benefit from it. It is a guide for every situation and every kind of society. In this speech there is guidance, interest and knowledge for every person, every soul, and every level of intellect and understanding. Every person can benefit from it according to his capacity for intellectual digestion. As humanity advances through stages of progress in knowledge and recognition, as its circle of understanding widens, its information increases, its experiences move forward, and it attains the secrets of the self and the universe, its share in this Qur'an also increases. Its knowledge of the Qur'an increases, its provision and its sustenance from this Qur'an grow. This is the Book "whose wonders never end, and which does not become old through much use." These are the words that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said about it, because the one most familiar with its secrets and subtleties is the Messenger himself. This was the living experience that he had with the Qur'an, and which he expressed in these words (ﷺ).

Those who first heard the Qur'an understood the proofs and signs present in this universe, and the proofs and signs within their own souls, according to the knowledge and recognition of their time. The generations that came after them also understood and explained these verses according to their knowledge, recognition and experiences. Today we too are receiving our share, to the extent of the knowledge, recognition, experiences and discoveries that have come to us until now. The sciences and experiences that have reached us today are a very small part of the signs of this great universe and of the intricate human soul. Future generations will find more signs than we have. In this universe and in the human soul, and until the Day of Resurrection, new wonders will continue to be placed on display in this exhibition hall of the world and this exhibition hall of the human self.

This earth, a planet prepared for life, which is the cradle of life and has been equipped with all the necessities of life, and it appears that perhaps in this vast and terrifying universe it is the only planet prepared for existence. In it there are stars that stay in one place, and planets that move in orbits. Of those that we know, their number runs into billions, and it must be remembered that the part of the universe that is known is comparatively very small. In it there are several million galaxies, and each galaxy has tens of millions of stars, and around these stars there are celestial bodies that keep revolving.

Of these planets, only this earth is a planet which has been given wonderful characteristics for the life upon it. Each of these characteristics is a sign. If even one of these characteristics were to disappear or undergo some alteration, all kinds of life would cease to exist upon the earth. If the size of this earth were to change, became tilted, or smaller; if its distance from the sun were to change, decrease or increase; if the size of the sun were to change and its temperature were to change; and if the inclination of this earth on its axis, as it is tilted, were to undergo any variation; if its axial rotation or its annual revolution around the sun were to fluctuate; if the size of the moon were to vary or it were to come nearer to or farther from the earth; if the proportion of land and water on the earth were to change; in short, if, if, if.... and thousands of ifs, if any one of these thousands of harmonies and facilities were to change, then the very trace of this beautiful life on this planet would vanish.

Is this not one sign? Are not all these things signs which show that there is a Being who has arranged them, and provided for them?

And the various kinds of food and sustenance which Allah has provided for the creatures that live and dwell on this earth. Whether these creatures live on the surface of the earth, swim in the air, swim in the water, live in the caves of the earth, dwell in its mountains, or reside within its valleys and settlements, food is prepared for all of them. For some it is in compound form, and for some in simple form. In any case, it is acceptable for the existence of these living things and fulfils the needs of these countless living beings. Just as living creatures are of countless kinds and varieties, so too their food is of countless kinds and varieties. These kinds of food that are within the earth, that flow and move, that are in the air, that grow upon the surface of the earth, that come from the sun, that come from other worlds, and that you do not even know of; yet every kind of food is coming to these living things from every direction, and in great quantity. According to the will of Allah and His management, this is a great treasure and storehouse which supplies the provision for these countless kinds of eaters. This is the arrangement of the Divine Storehouse of the Provider.

Then the variety of the sights and scenes of this earth, wherever the eye can reach and wherever feet can go, these too are wonders in their own right, which do not cease. These narrow pits and wide streams, valleys and mountains, seas and lakes, rivers and canals, and patches of gardens, grapes and dates, single and double-stemmed; all these scenes and sights are such that they show that they are a marvel of the perfections of the Maker. In them there are constant changes, and they never remain in one state. A person passes over a land and sees it dry and stricken by famine; this too is a scene. Then he sees it green and full of blessings and fodder; this too is a scene. At times he sees it in the greatest greenness and delight; this is a scene. At times he sees that the whole earth has turned yellow and dry and the harvest is about to be cut; this too is a scene, and he stands in his place, having not gone here or there at all.

All those creatures which are populating this earth, such as living creatures, plants and animals, fish and birds, cattle and insects, and humans, the Qur'an has mentioned them in a single verse.

These creatures, of whose kinds and varieties we do not fully have knowledge, it is far-fetched that the individuals of a single kind could be counted. That is impossible. Each kind of these creatures is a community, and each individual of them is a marvel. Every animal, every bird, every beast and every insect, every plant; not only that, but every branch of every plant, and every leaf of every branch, and every flower of every branch, and every petal of every flower: this is an exhibition hall of Allah whose wonders never end.

If human beings were to begin to describe, nay, if all human beings were to describe at the same time, and were to reflect, write and speak about what signs of Allah and what wonders are in this earth, then neither would their account come to an end, nor would the wonders and indications come to an end. This verse of the Qur'an only explains this much: that the heart and mind of a human being should be awakened to reflection, and should see the things that nature has placed in this magnificent exhibition, and bring them into the light, understand them and make them understood, laugh and make others laugh, and thus make this brief journey upon this earth pleasant.

But the real truth is that only the one whose heart has been filled with certainty can perceive these wonders, and only he can make this brief journey of life pleasant through them.

﴿And in the earth are signs for those who have certainty﴾ (51:20) "And in the earth are signs for those who are certain." It is certainty that provides eyes with sight, so that they see. It is faith that gives life to these manifestations of divine power in the earth, and they reveal their secrets and mysteries, and show what the works of the hand of divine power are behind them. Without faith, all these scenes and sights remain dead, become rigid, and are empty of meaning. They do not converse with a heart that is devoid of faith; they do not walk alongside it. There are many people who walk about in this exhibition hall of Allah, yet they see nothing in it. This universe does not appear to them as alive and speaking. They do not understand its language, because their hearts have not been given life by the touch of faith. For them their environment is not alive. Among such people there may be great scholars and scientists as well.

﴿They know only an outward appearance of the worldly life﴾ (30:7) "But they know only the outward appearance of the life of this world." As for the inner reality of this world, it is hidden from their sight, because any heart can unlock the reality of this universe with the key of faith; any eye can see these realities only with the light of faith. ﴿Sadaqa Allahu al-'Azim﴾ ........

Now, from among these wonders, the second marvel.

"And in yourselves. Will you not then see?" (51:21). This human being is indeed a great marvel among the wonders of the universe, but what is his destiny? What is his station, and what secrets and mysteries lie within his being? He is heedless of them, and he is heedless because he is deprived of the blessing of faith and certainty.

This human being is a marvel in his bodily structure. He is a marvel in the secrets of the body. He is a marvel in the spiritual world. The realm of the psyche is entirely its own. In short, he is a marvel in his outward and in his inward being. This human being is a sample of the elements of this universe, and the secrets and mysteries of the entire universe lie hidden within him.

"You think yourself a small particle,
yet within you the greater world is enfolded."

When a person observes the wonders of his own self and his own soul, he is left astonished and bewildered. The formation and arrangement of his organs, then the functions of those organs and their activity within: for example, the process of obtaining nourishment and food, the process of breathing and the process of burning, the flow of blood in the heart and arteries, the nervous system and how it runs the whole body, the glands and how they run and develop the body; then the harmony, unity and coordination of all these things and their moving perfectly in step together. Then, within these wonders are detailed wonders, and within every part are extraordinary marvels, each of which is awe-inspiring.

Then there are the spiritual powers of the human being, some of which are known and some of which are unknown. His perception of things, and then the mechanism of perception; then the retention of what has been perceived, and afterwards the recalling of it. These images in the treasury of knowledge and the mind: where are they, and how are they preserved? These pictures, these representations, these observations and their impressions: how are they imprinted, and how are these images formed? These are the aspects of those powers that are known to us. As for those powers that are not known to us, they are very great indeed. Very great. Sometimes their traces become apparent. Sometimes a illumination and a light is cast upon the human mind, and within it such a radiance arises that the unseen world opens up to a person far and wide; but such moments are rare.

Then there are the secrets and mysteries of human reproduction. A very tiny cell within which all the characteristics of the human species are present, and within which are also present the characteristics of the father, the mother, and close relatives on both sides. Where and how are all these characteristics placed within that very tiny cell, and how does each cell, with all these characteristics, begin its journey of life in an automatic manner, such that within it are all the characteristics of the human species, and it fully reproduces the human species in the form of another individual?!!

The moments in which a child begins life upon this earth, separates from its mother, and begins to live by trusting its own self, and its heart and lungs are permitted to move. Merely by reflecting a little upon these moments, a person becomes astonished and even stunned, and the intellect is dumbfounded. The human soul is filled with wonder and amazement, and then it is also filled with faith. This is such a scene that the heart and mind of a person stop functioning because of amazement. A person is left bewildered.

Then, that time too is worth seeing, when the child begins to speak in broken language, then forms words and sentences. Indeed, just consider speech alone. The producing of separate sounds from the tongue, and then sounds from the throat: this too is a marvel. We do not perceive the strangeness of this because people are always speaking, but if a person reflects on it for a single moment, then the mere ability of a human being to express what is in his heart is itself a marvel, and is a clear and sufficient proof of divine power.

In short, even a partial event in human life is a miracle, and a person can be amazed by it; and this is the meaning of the following phrase:

"And in yourselves. Will you not then see?" (51:21). Each single individual of the human species is also a world. Every individual is a mirror in which this entire universe is seen, and within the being of every individual this whole world is, as it were, manifested again and again. Every person is entirely distinct from his fellow humans in his face, his features, his intellect, his knowledge, his perceptions, his soul and his consciousness. The conception of the universe held in each person's mind differs from that of others. Now consider: in this divine exhibition hall there are millions of individuals, each one a unique specimen, each one's temperament entirely different, and no such person is ever created again. The whole universe passes through that person, and his form cannot be reproduced. Even the lines of the fingerprints are different for every person in the world, and they cannot be repeated. Among those who have passed in bygone ages too, the fingerprint lines of none can be repeated.

Among the wonders of the human species, many are those that lie before our eyes, and our eyes are seeing them.

"And in yourselves. Will you not then see?" (51:21)

And whatever wonders human eyes behold, they point towards the unseen world, that they are signs of a Creator who fashioned them.

The wonders and miracles within the human self cannot be recorded in a single book. Even for those wonders that have so far become known to us and whose disclosure has taken place, several volumes are required; and as for those that remain unknown, the experience of the past shows that they are very many. The Holy Qur'an has not enumerated them. Yet the Holy Qur'an has certainly shaken the heart and mind, saying: awake, and reflect, be conscious and understand; walk with open eyes through this wondrous house of God. Reflect, and before this universe, reflect upon your own self. Just as you are heedless of the horizons, you are likewise heedless of your own being.

The truth is that the most pleasant moments of life are those in which a person reflects upon his own creation, his own qualities, his features, his movements and his habits, and tours this wondrous house of God like a devoted servant, and sees how blessed God is. Yet man spends a long life in this wondrous house and spends it without awareness.

Thus, by bestowing awareness, the Holy Qur'an grants man an entirely new life: a new consciousness, a new way of thinking, a new life. And this consciousness is a precious provision of life, such that no other blessing of this world is worth anything in comparison with it.

The Qur'an trains a person with this method of contemplation and perception, but the fundamental point of this training is faith. Without faith, the Qur'an cannot be received by a person in what it wishes to give him. It is faith alone that makes a person worthy of this provision of life. It is an exceedingly lofty, superior and heavenly provision of life. A person's feet are upon the earth, while his consciousness dwells in the higher realm.

First, man was shown a glimpse of the universe; then he was shown a glimpse of the wonders of his own self. Now it is stated that the provision of man, its distribution and his allotted share are also distributed from the heavens, and your final destination too is in the heavens.

﴿And in the heaven is your provision, and that which you are promised.﴾ (51:22)

Apparently, this is a strange guidance and a signal that draws attention. Although the means of provision are on the earth, and a person strives within those means and arranges his provision through that effort, the Qur'an turns human eyes towards the heavens. It leads from the visible world to the unseen world, so that a person may hope for his share of provision there. As for the fact that the earth and the means within it have been placed here, these are signs for those who have certainty. By seeing these signs and marks, a person turns towards Allah, so that he may hope for a better provision from Allah and be free from the burden of the earth and its lowliness. In this way, he is also free from the apparent means of provision. Let it not be that these apparent means come between a person and the Creator of the means, and he becomes lost within those apparent means.

The heart of the believer takes this guidance as a reality. He also understands it. He knows that the purpose of this guidance is not that the earth and its means should be disregarded, because a person is responsible for putting the means of the earth to use and for fulfilling, here on the earth, the duties of the vicegerency (khilafah) of Allah. The purpose is that he should not bind his heart to the means of the earth, nor forget God while engaged in the building and development of this earth. Rather, his attitude should be that he works on the earth while his eyes are on the heavens. He should employ the means, but he should be certain that those means are not his duties, rather the Provider is in the heavens, this is Allah's promise, and what happens is exactly what Allah has said.

Thus, the heart of a believer is freed from the grip of the means that are on the earth, rather, through those very means he reaches the kingdom of the heavens. When he sees that within these means there are wonders which point to the Creator of the means, he attains access to God through them. Although his feet are on the earth, within those very means, his eyes are upon the heavens. This is the method that Allah has chosen for humanity, and this is the method that Allah has prescribed for those servants whom He created from clay, breathed into them of His spirit, and gave them preference over all the creatures of this world.

Faith is a means and a cause for a person to be in the best circumstances of life. When a person is in a state of faith, he is in the state in which Allah created him. It is upon the fitrah (natural disposition) of Allah upon which He created him. States of corruption and deviation come upon a person afterwards.

After drawing attention to these three glimpses, namely the signs of the earth, the signs of the self, and the signs of the heavens, Allah, by swearing by His own Being, assures that these matters are as true as your own speech.

﴿So by the Lord of the heaven and the earth, indeed it is the truth, just as [certain] as your speech.﴾ (51:32)

That they are sitting and engaged in conversation is a reality. There is no doubt that this is a reality, and there is no room for dispute about it. Likewise, this speech is a certain speech, and Allah is the most truthful.

Al-Asma'i (a famous philologist) narrated a strange account, and ʿAllamah Zamakhshari (Al-Kashshaf) has also reported it in his Kashshaf. While keeping reservations about the soundness of the narration, we cite it here because the account is very strange. It is said: "I was returning from the Jami' Mosque of Basra when a Bedouin appeared on his riding camel. He said, 'To which tribe do you belong?' I said, 'To the Banu Asma'.' He said, 'Where have you come from?' I said, 'From a place where the speech of the Most Merciful is recited.' He said, 'Then recite to me.' So I recited.

﴿By the scatterers [of dust] ... ﴾ (51:1–22) ... until I reached this point.

﴿And in the heaven is your provision and that which you are promised.﴾ (51:22)

He said, 'That is enough.' He stood up, slaughtered his camel and distributed its meat to those passing along the road. He then struck his sword and arrow against the ground, broke them, and departed. Then, when I was performing the tawaf with Harun al-Rashid at dawn, I saw that very same man speaking gently with me. I recognized him as that same Bedouin; he was thin and yellowish in complexion. He greeted me when I reached this spot:

﴿And that which you are promised﴾ (51:22), up to this point, he called out loudly: 'Indeed, what our Lord promised us, I have found it.' Then he said, 'Is there anything beyond this?' So I recited:

﴿So by the Lord of the heaven and the earth, indeed it is the truth.﴾ (51:23)

That man raised his voice and said, 'Subhan Allah! Who was it that angered the Lord of Majesty so much that He had to swear an oath? They did not affirm the word of Allah, until they compelled the Lord to swear.' He said this three times, and then his soul departed."

This is a strange story. Whether it is authentic or not, we have cited it here so that, because the Lord of Majesty has sworn by it, the importance of what He swore upon becomes even greater, although that great reality is true even without an oath or swearing.

This was the first part of this surah. In the second part there are brief allusions to the stories of Ibrahim, Lut, Musa, the people of ʿAd (the people of Hud), the people of Thamud (the people of Salih), and Nuh (peace be upon them). This part is also connected to what precedes and follows it.

This second part also recounts, from the history of the prophets, the signs of Allah, just as the first part mentioned the cosmic signs (ayat takwini) and the signs within the self (ayat fi'l-nafs). These too were Allah's true promises, and they took on the form of reality, just as the true promise of Allah was mentioned in the first part.

The discussion opens with a question concerning the guests of Ibrahim (Abraham, peace be upon him).

﴿Has there come to you the story of the honoured guests of Ibrahim?﴾ (51:24) "O Prophet, has the account of the honoured guests of Ibrahim ... reached you?" This question points to the need to prepare and draw the minds toward this account. The word "mukramin" (honoured) is used for the guests, either because they were honoured and esteemed in the sight of Allah, or to indicate that they were honoured guests of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), and that he showed them honour.

From this incident it becomes clear how generous and liberal Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was, and how he would spend his wealth lavishly in hospitality. Some Muslims came from that direction, greeted him, and he returned their greeting. He did not recognise these guests, and after the exchange of greetings he went to his wife and ordered her to prepare a meal. This food too was prepared in an instant, and quickly a large quantity of roasted calf was placed before the guests, which was enough for dozens of people.

"So his wife came forward, crying out, and struck her face and said, 'An old barren woman!'" (15:92) She had heard this good news, yet suddenly, on hearing it, she gave a cry, and in keeping with the habit of women she struck her face and said that she was an old woman and barren. All these things were a source of pleasant astonishment to her. In truth she was barren, and this news was an unexpected joyful tidings that she had never anticipated. But she forgot that it was the angels who were giving this good news, so the angels drew her attention to the fact that this is the power of Allah, and that in the world all matters take place in accordance with the knowledge of Allah.

"They said, 'So has your Lord said. Indeed, He is the Wise, the All-Knowing.'" That is: when Allah says of something, "Be," it comes to be, and since Allah has said this, what room is there for doubt after it?

Being accustomed to a matter, and having it constantly before one's eyes, are things that shackle human perception and confine a person's conception of things. Then, when a person sees something different from this familiar and routine course of affairs, he is stunned and wonders how it has come about. Sometimes, out of arrogance, he then denies it. But the will of Allah takes its own course; He is not bound by the familiar habits of people. The sphere of human perception and the sphere of ordinary affairs are very limited, whereas the powers of Allah are very vast (extended).

Verse 31 of Surah 51 (adh-Dhariyat) is the verse the commentary is on, and the passage begins with Ibrahim (peace be upon him) learning the true identity of his guests and asking about their mission. I'll translate the text as given.

When Ibrahim (peace be upon him) had ascertained the reality of his guests, they began to ask what their mission was.

﴿Qala innā ursilnā ilā qawmin mujrimīn﴾ (15:13) "He said: 'O messengers of God, what is your urgent matter?' Then they gave their reply."
﴿They said, "We have indeed been sent to a criminal people."﴾ (15 : 23) This was the people of Lut, as is made explicit in other surahs.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 51, verses 33–34:

لنرسل ........ للمسرفین (15 : 43)

"So that We may send down upon them stones of baked clay, marked by your Lord for those who transgress beyond limits."

These clay stones were prepared and marked, and Allah had made them ready for the transgressors. The transgressing people were the people of Lut, who crossed the bounds and acted contrary to nature, going against the path of fitrah (natural disposition). It was a path opposed to truth and religion. Nothing prevents us from holding that these stones were rocks rained down as a result of volcanic activity, since molten lava, when it is thrown into the air, turns into stone. This was imposed by the Lord, operated according to His laws of power and the laws of nature, and fell upon the very person about whom the command of Allah had been issued. For every stone, Allah, by His knowledge, has determined a time and place, namely that at that place He would overtake a particular person. And Allah has decided that each stone should be hurled through the agency of angels. Then, we do not have full knowledge of the reality of angels, nor do we know what the relationship of angels is with this universe. Moreover, what is the reality of the forces that we know, whose manifestations are constantly before us, and to which we keep giving names of our own? We have no right to object to Allah's report that He imposed some of His forces upon some transgressors and did so in a particular place. In any case, we have no right to object to this report of Allah. This is because our information about this universe is very limited and based on hypotheses; indeed, these are theories, and merely superficial interpretations of these things. Up to now, there is little information that has become fact. In short, whether these were stones from volcanic activity or other stones, in any case they were a manifestation of the power of Divine hand, a product of His creative process, and how they were exactly is also a matter of the unseen.

Now, the second sign is in the story of Musa (Moses). Only a brief allusion is made to this story here, because the verses here recount the signposts of the path from the history of the prophets.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 51, verses 38–39:

The clear proof and authority with which Musa (peace be upon him) was sent was a plain and decisive proof, and there was the awe-inspiring dignity that was in the person of Hazrat Musa (peace be upon him). With Musa and Harun was the Divine Being, who hears and sees. But Pharaoh turned away in arrogance, and despite seeing the manifest truth and seeing the decisive proof, he resorted to evasion. He called Hazrat Musa, the Prophet of God, a sorcerer and a madman, although Musa had shown him miracles before which those people were left speechless. This conduct makes it known that when someone is not prepared for guidance, even the greatest miracle cannot be effective in bringing him to guidance, and a tongue that insists on falsehood cannot be silenced.

Here, in the context of the discourse, the details of this story are not given; rather, only its outcome is mentioned, which remains forever as a sign and a historical lesson from this story.

The Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 51, verse 40:

﴿Then We seized him and his hosts, and We threw them into the sea, and he was one who deserved blame.﴾ That is, because of his arrogance and his denial of the truth, he became deserving of blame.

The manner of expression clearly indicates that He Himself, directly, seized him and his hosts and cast them into the river. This aspect is highlighted so that the sign (ayah) in the story of Musa (peace be upon him) becomes apparent, because here God is enumerating His signs from the horizons, from the self, and from history. The stories of the messengers from history are, in fact, signposts on the way.

And another historical sign: a look at the people of ʿĀd.

"And in ʿĀd (there is a sign), when We sent upon them the barren wind (al-rīḥ al-ʿaqīm). It left nothing it passed over but that it made it like decayed bones" (Qur'an 51:41–42; cf. 15:24 for the wording "ما تذر ... كالرميم").

The wind sent upon the people of ʿĀd is called here ʿaqīm (barren). This is because that wind had neither water in it nor anything of goodness that could be a means of life, as the people of ʿĀd had expected from the wind. On the contrary, it carried only destruction and ruin. Whatever it touched, it reduced to lifelessness, just as a dead thing decays and crumbles into pieces. The wind is one of the cosmic forces, and it is one of the armies of Allah, and none knows the armies of Allah except Allah Himself. Allah sends these armies within the bounds of His will and His established order, and the manner in which these armies work differs. When they fall upon a people, they do so by Allah's will and at His appointed time: they destroy and annihilate some, and they bring life and radiance to others. Therefore, in such matters, no one has the right to raise those superficial and simplistic objections, saying that the wind moves according to the cosmic system and that it blows here and there according to physical causes and factors. We say that this natural system and these cosmic factors are also driven by the Creator; with His planning and decree, He destroys some and gives life to others. These factors are of His creation, the means are His, and the physical laws were established by Him, and with them He imposes these factors upon whomever He wills. If someone believes in the Creator of the universe, then there is no room for such objections.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 51, verses 43–44:

And the third sign is the people of Thamud:

﴿And in Thamud, when it was said to them, "Enjoy yourselves for a while." But they defied the command of their Lord, so the thunderbolt seized them while they looked on. Then they could not rise up, nor could they defend themselves.﴾ (15:14 to 54)

The words ﴿Enjoy yourselves for a while﴾ (15:34) may also mean that they were given a respite of three days, as is stated elsewhere: ﴿Then Salih said to them, "Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days"﴾, and that period may be meant here as well, namely the time from the commencement of the Prophet's mission (risalah) until the killing of the she-camel, when they disobeyed the command of God by slaying the she-camel and their destruction was decreed.

Regarding the rain of stones upon the people of Lut, what we have said about them applies equally to the wind sent upon the people of 'Ad and to the cry that came upon the people of Thamud. These are all cosmic forces, controlled by God's providence. They operate in accordance with His will and His laws, and within the bounds of those laws God imposes them as a punishment upon whichever people He wills. Thus these forces do only what God assigns to them, and the hosts of God are countless and incomparable.

﴿And before them, We destroyed the people of Noah, for they were a transgressing people.﴾ (15:64)

This account of Noah is a very brief allusion, without details and without additions, as if to say: "Remember the people of Noah too." In the story of Noah, where the Qur'an uses the words "فی نوح" (fī Nūḥ, "concerning Noah"), the original phrasing is instead "قوم نوح" (qawm Nūḥ, "the people of Noah"). The original sentence is: "اذکرقوم نوح" (udhkur qawma Nūḥ, "Remember the people of Noah"), so that the people of Noah are mentioned, and after this the verses begin.

The construction "wa-al-sama' banaynaha" is conjoined to it (the preceding clause), so the sign of the people of Nuh is a historical sign, and the sign of the sky is a cosmic (takwini) sign. Here both have been linked together by the conjunction particle, and through these two the present passage has been connected with the third passage of this surah.

Now the discourse returns to the exhibition of this universe with which this surah opened. The universe holds many images that polish the heart and sight, and now a new picture from the album of this universe is brought before you, and through it you are advised to seek the signs of Allah in this exhibition-hall of the cosmos. Thus the sign of the story of Prophet Nuh now combines with the pictorial narratives of the heavens and the earth, and after this people are once again called in a loud voice: Hasten towards Allah! With the pure doctrine of Tawhid.

﴿وَالسَّمَاءَ بَنَيْنَاهَا بِأَيْيْدٍ وَإِنَّا لَمُوسِعُونَ﴾ (15 : 74) "And the heaven We built with power, and indeed We are expanding it."

Al-aid (الايد) refers to power. The creation of the vast, awe-inspiring and expansive heavens, and their sustenance under control, is itself the manifestation of Allah's great power. Whatever you take the word "sky" (al-sama') to mean, whether you take it to mean the orbits of the planets, or the galaxy (kahkashan), a cluster of stars containing many millions of stars, or the layers of the high atmosphere within which these stars and planets are scattered, or any other meaning of this word, in any case this is a wonder of divine power.

Similarly, expansiveness (al-si'ah) may also mean these planets, which are of enormous size and number in the millions, and are scattered in this awe-inspiring and dizzying expanse of the cosmos, just as particles are scattered. That alone is the expansiveness.

It is also possible that expansiveness means the treasures which Allah has kept for the sustenance and food of human beings, and these treasures are in the heavens. In this surah, "sky" here will mean only that which is with Allah. But the manner of expression of the Qur'an is such that within it there is an allusion to the meaning of a word. This meaning is cast as a shadow over the expression, and this is done deliberately so that human consciousness may be impressed by it.

The passage also draws attention here to the earth spread out as a carpet.

"And the earth – We have spread it out, and how excellent a spreader We are!" (Qur'an 15:84)

God prepared this earth so that it would serve as a cradle for life, just as We have already explained in detail. A carpet is a source of comfort and ease for a person. The earth has been prepared, leveled and made into a place of convenience and a cradle of life. For this reason it has been described as a carpet. Every part of it has been prepared, with the utmost depth, for the sustenance of life.

"How excellent a spreader We are!" (Qur'an 15:84)

**Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 51, verses 49–50:**

﴿And of everything We created pairs, that you may remember.﴾ (15:94)

This is a remarkable fact that describes the basic principle of the creation of this earth. It is possible that this same principle operates throughout the entire universe, since nothing in the wording indicates that it operates only on the earth. The principle of pairing (zawjiyyat) in creation is clearly visible in living things. But the word "shay'" (thing) also applies to other things, which means that all things are also created on the principle of pairing.

When we keep in mind that we have been reciting this verse for fourteen hundred years, and that the idea of such all-encompassing pairing in creation was not known then as it is known now, we see that even in living things this principle was not conceived as so pervasive, let alone that anyone would imagine pairing within all things. If we consider this reality, a marvel stands before us, and it tells us that everything in this entire universe is based on the principle of pairing.

This verse also points to a reality: the discoveries of the modern age are bringing us very close to the great truth. All research is increasingly agreeing that creation in the universe proceeds from the atom, and that the atom is composed of two electrical pairs, positive and negative. Modern physical research is therefore moving toward proof of this truth.

In the light of expressions that are small and brief in wording but great and astonishing in meaning, and in the light of the dialogue and observation of the vastness of the heavens, the surroundings of the earth, and the souls of creatures, Allah now calls out to His creation in a very loud voice: run toward the Creator of the earth and the heavens, sincerely, casting every burden from your shoulders, with a light spirit, a free heart, and the banner of Tawhid in your hands.

Describing the coming to Allah as "flight" (firar) is in fact a strange and meaningful expression. Especially through the greed for sustenance and wealth, and in order to obtain their share of provision, people have been absorbed in the apparent means of livelihood. Therefore, to free people from these bonds, a very forceful call and a loud summons were needed, and in the choice of words such a word was taken that means "run with intensity," and run towards Allah without associating anyone with Him, and it was said to complete the proof.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 51, verses 52–54:

Thus it has been: no messenger came to those before them but they said, "A sorcerer or a madman." Have they bequeathed this to one another? Nay, they are a people who transgress. So turn away from them, and you are not to be blamed. But remind, for the reminder benefits the believers. (Qur'an 51:52–55, as quoted in the Urdu text, with the verse numbering as given there: 15:25 to 15:55)

The opposition of all the messengers' opponents and deniers has been of one nature. The misguided have always shown a similar reaction against the call of the messengers.

Thus it has been, "no messenger came to those before them but they said, 'A sorcerer or a madman'" (Qur'an 51:52 / 15:25 as cited).

Just as the Quraysh of Makkah are saying now. It is as if the disbelievers of earlier and later times had consulted with one another. They did not actually consult together, but rebellion, misguidance and the disposition to oppression are of one kind, so the earlier and later ones have gathered upon this same course.

The result that follows from the continuous single stance of the deniers is that the Messenger (ﷺ) should not care about their denial. These people have, as it were, agreed upon this attitude, so the Messenger (ﷺ) is not blameworthy for it. He should not concern himself with it. He is only a reminder, and he should continue to remind, even though people object and turn away.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 51, verse 56:

وما خلقت ........ المتین (85) (15:65 to 85)

"I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me. I do not seek any provision from them, nor do I want them to feed Me. Indeed, Allah is the Provider, the Possessor of strength, the Mighty."

This short verse in fact contains a great truth. It is that truth of this universe upon which human life cannot be correct except by acting upon it, whether individual life, collective life, or global life, and in every age this truth has remained true and will remain so.

This great truth unfolds the most important aspects and hidden meanings of the human world, and these meanings and aspects are those upon which the whole collective life rests.

Its first aspect is that the specific purpose of the existence of jinn and mankind is that Allah be worshipped. For this purpose Allah has prescribed certain obligations. Whoever fulfils these obligations has, as it were, attained the purpose of life. Whoever neglects these obligations or turns away from them has, as it were, lost the purpose of life, and that person becomes purposeless and useless, his life becomes meaningless, and he has no value left, because life can become meaningful only through this purpose. Such a person has stepped out of the natural order (namoos-e-fitrat) for which Allah created him, and he is, as it were, completely lost, just as everything that gives up performing its appointed duty becomes useless, because the purpose of life is in truth the guarantor of a person's survival. A thing that does not fulfil its purpose of existence becomes worthless even if it remains alive or present. What is this purpose of life that connects jinn and mankind to the natural order? It is the worship of Allah, that is, there will be a servant (bandah) and there will be his Lord. The servant will worship, and his Lord will be the one worshipped, and the whole life of the servant must be arranged according to this purpose. In other words, the 'abd (servant) must render complete worship to the Ma'bud (the One worshipped).

Here the second aspect of this great truth comes before us. It is that worship means worship throughout one's whole life, and worship does not mean only the forms of servitude or the methods of devotion, but its meaning is very broad, because jinn and mankind do not spend their entire lives, night and day, only in worship. Allah has not obligated people to worship and serve Him night and day, but He has obligated them to lead various kinds of life. We do not know the activities of the jinn, but we do know the activities of humans. The Qur'an has described the scheme of the creation of man.

"And when your Lord said to the angels, 'Indeed I will make upon the earth a khalifah (vicegerent).'"

Therefore, the discharge of the duty of khilafah (vicegerency) on earth is also the responsibility of man, and the responsibility of khilafah includes various kinds of activities, that is, exercising control over the forces of the earth, searching out the treasures hidden within it and using them for the service of humanity, developing human life upon the earth. Thus among the responsibilities of khilafah is also this: that those who are Muslims should establish the Shari'ah of Allah, and just as Allah's will prevails in the universe, in the same way His will should be enforced in the voluntary life of man.

From this it becomes clear that the act of worship, which is the purpose of human life, has a broader and more comprehensive meaning, and it does not refer only to the forms of servitude, and carrying out the duties of Allah's khilafah on earth is also included in worship. Therefore, Islamic worship has two aspects.

1. The first is that the meaning of Allah's servitude should be fully settled in the mind. This is the conscious affirmation that there is a servant who worships and a Lord who is worshipped, and there is nothing beyond this. On one side is servitude and slavery, and on the other side is the Master and Creator. Here is the 'abd, there is the Ma'bud. The Lord is One; no one shares with Him, and all creation other than Him are worshippers and slaves.

2. The second aspect of this supreme truth is that a person turns every inner movement of the heart, every attention, and every physical movement and its direction towards Allah at every turn of life. He should be directed only to Allah, remove from his heart every consciousness other than Allah, and exclude from his life every movement other than the worship of Allah.

From these two aspects the concept of worship comes fully into being, every action becomes an act of worship, and the forms of servitude take shape in such a way that, just as someone is engaged in the construction and development of this earth, then the work of building and developing the earth becomes jihad fi sabilillah, and jihad fi sabilillah happens in the way that a person patiently endures difficulties. (That is, every movement and every work of life becomes worship.) And all these works are fulfilling the purpose for which Allah created jinn and mankind, and the purpose which the whole universe is fulfilling.

When this doctrine and belief settle in a mind, it becomes certain of the purpose for which Allah has created it in this world. It has come here so that in this brief portion of life it may discharge this obligation: the service of Allah, the worship of Allah, and nothing else as its purpose. It should be content with this. It should be satisfied with its deeds and its circumstances, that Allah is pleased with it. As for the individual reward, that will be a grace and bounty of Allah.

If a person reaches this stage, it can be said that he has truly run towards Allah. Having passed over the lowliness of this earth, its obstacles and all its entanglements, and having freed himself from everything, he has adopted flight towards Allah. Through this freedom he has become free from all the restrictions of the earth, and has become devoted to Allah, and he has arrived at the true station of this universe, that is, the station of servitude to Allah for which Allah created him. Now he has stood up at his proper place. He has fulfilled his purpose of existence. Therefore, among the requirements of the worship of Allah is this requirement too: that a person also fulfils the duties of khilafah on this earth. He should discharge his responsibilities here, benefit from the fruits of this earth to the utmost limit, but in a state in which he is shaking his hands free of them, and his heart is detached and indifferent to the deceptive and alluring things of this earth. In such a way that he is not gathering the fruits and pleasures of this world solely for his own self, but is doing so as a duty of life, as worship, and as flight to Allah, and is doing so only to the extent of necessity.

One of the results of this concept and this great truth is that a person does not keep his eye on the results of his deeds, but looks at the intention with which he performs them. Whatever the results may be, a person is not responsible for the results. He is responsible only for obeying the command and for worship, because his reward is not his deeds' results, but rather his reward is that he is serving or is not serving.

After attaining this supreme truth, a person's outlook on duties, obligations and actions suddenly changes. In every task he sees whether he is fulfilling the duty of worship or not. When he sees that he has performed the worship, his task is finished. Now whatever the results may be, let them be, because the results of actions do not fall within his duties, nor is it within his power to produce results, since results are to emerge according to Allah's will and decree. His striving, his intention, and his action are the manifestation of the divine decree.

When a person strives in this sense, and lets go of results, and attains the awareness that he has done his part, and that his recompense is with Allah, because his task was to obey Allah's command, then he no longer has any desire regarding this world. He harbours no enmity towards anyone for any worldly purpose, and there is no longing in his heart for any worldly aim. He has striven according to his capacity. He has discharged his responsibilities in this world and fulfilled his share of duties, and he has shaken his hands free of the results and aims of this world, and he has removed from his heart the desire to obtain the fruits of his striving, because when he has performed worship, its fruit has been attained. As for personal interests, these were never his purpose.

The Qur'an nourishes this kind of feeling and strengthens such concepts. It teaches a person: do not grieve over provision; the responsibility for provision lies with Allah. Allah has taken upon Himself the responsibility for the provision of His servants. Allah Himself is not in need of any provision or food. He has made these arrangements for His servants. The commands Allah gives to people regarding spending upon the needy and the poor are also for their own benefit.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 51, verses 57–59:

"I do not want any provision from them, nor do I want them to feed Me. Indeed, Allah is the Provider, the Possessor of strength, the Mighty." (51:57–58)

In performing the duties of vicegerency (khilafah) on this earth, a believer does not have merely the drive to earn sustenance. Rather, this drive is the drive of servitude to Allah, and worship is fulfilled only when a person strives with all his effort in this world while acknowledging the command of Allah. Therefore, behind the striving of a believer here lies the spirit of Allah's servitude and obedience, and in this spirit none of the worldly interests is present at all, because striving for lofty aims in this world is a great and elevated act, and it can only be undertaken under a lofty concept and spirit.

Today, if humanity is deprived of that lofty provision, it is deprived because the people are not living under the teachings of the Quran as the Muslims of the first era used to live, and they have not derived their principles of life from the Quranic constitution.

When a person or a society rises to that horizon, that is, the horizon of servitude and bondage (to Allah), and becomes firmly established upon it, then their self-respect refuses to achieve any lofty objective through any base means, even if that objective is the exaltation of Islam and the dominance of Islam, because base means nullify the pure objective of the servitude of Allah. Moreover, when someone reaches that station, he does not worry about delivering the self to its destination; rather, he is preoccupied with the concern of whether he has fulfilled his duty or not, that is, while grasping the meaning and the great reality of the servitude of Allah. As far as the attainment of objectives is concerned, that is in Allah's hands. The results that Allah has determined in His decree will become manifest through the hidden decree. Therefore, we should not seek to adopt wrong means to achieve results, since the manifestation of results is in Allah's hand, and it is not the responsibility of a believer who only serves Allah.

The conscience of the worshipper is at peace, his self is steadfast, and his heart is sound and secure in all circumstances, whether he sees the fruits of his deeds or not, and whether these results accord with his intention and action or turn out contrary to them, because according to this meaning of worship he has done his work. Allah has given the guarantee of his reward. Now he is joyful and content. What happens in practice after this lies outside the sphere of his duties, because he has declared that he is a servant; therefore, in terms of his understanding and thought, or in terms of his proposals and demands, he cannot go beyond the limits of servitude. He has come to know that Allah is the Lord, so he does not take interest in the matters that fall within the domain of the Lord of the worlds. If his emotions stop here, Allah is pleased with him, and he is pleased with Allah.

These are some aspects of the great reality that has been stated in this verse. It is an extremely brief verse.

"And I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me." (51:56) When this reality settles in someone's heart and mind, it transforms the picture of that person's life.

Finally, in the light of this reality, the wrongdoers who do not believe, who deny the Hereafter and who hasten its coming are warned. The surah concludes with this powerful warning.
